title: GPU boxes, then: drivers, DKMS, CUDA and shared notebooks
part: Part 2 · Linux under AI systems, then and now
brief: The ML servers of the last decade are still in every company: a kernel module, a driver, a toolkit, a notebook server and a scheduler, each with its own way to break.

exercises.prompt: nvidia-smi says 'CUDA Version: 12.4' and nvcc --version says 11.8. Which one is wrong?
options: Neither: nvidia-smi shows the newest CUDA version the driver supports, nvcc shows the installed toolkit, and 11.8 runs on a 12.4-capable driver
exercises.explain: The driver and the toolkit are separate installs. A toolkit at or below the driver's supported version works; a newer toolkit than the driver supports does not.

exercises.prompt: Which command shows whether the NVIDIA module has been built for each installed kernel?
exercises.explain: It lists module, version, kernel and state (installed, built, or missing) for every kernel on the box.

exercises.prompt: This modprobe file blacklists the wrong driver. Before NVIDIA's driver is installed, nouveau must not load and must not set a display mode.
exercises.hint: blacklist nouveau, and options nouveau modeset=0. Then rebuild the initramfs (update-initramfs -u or dracut --force) and reboot.
exercises.explain: Two drivers cannot own the same GPU. Rebuild the initramfs so nouveau is not loaded at early boot. Distribution packages of the NVIDIA driver usually install this file for you; knowing it exists is what saves you when they did not.

checks.name: the NVIDIA driver itself is not blacklisted
nouveau does not set a display mode

exercises.prompt: A data scientist starts `jupyter lab --ip 0.0.0.0` on the shared GPU box with the token turned off. What did they just give the network?
options: A shell as their user on the GPU box: Jupyter runs arbitrary code and can open terminals
exercises.explain: Bind it to localhost and tunnel (ssh -L 8888:localhost:8888), or put JupyterHub with real authentication in front. Exposed notebooks were a way into ML boxes long before exposed LLM servers.

exercises.prompt: On a headless GPU server, the first CUDA call after the GPUs sit idle takes several seconds. What is the usual fix?
options: Run nvidia-persistenced, so the driver keeps the GPUs initialized when no process is using them
exercises.explain: Without a client holding the device, the driver tears down GPU state and rebuilds it on next use. NVIDIA recommends the persistence daemon on headless Linux systems.

exercises.prompt: A training job on a shared Slurm cluster dies with an 'oom-kill event', although the node has hundreds of GB free. Why?
options: The job used more than it requested (--mem); Slurm confines each job in a cgroup and the kernel enforces that limit
The GPU ran out of memory
exercises.explain: With cgroup confinement the requested memory is the job's hard limit. Size requests from evidence: sacct shows MaxRSS for past runs. A GPU running out of memory fails with a CUDA error, not a kernel OOM kill.
